raw_response:
I’m farming the same 10.1 mu in wheat-maize rotation again this year. That’s what works best for my land and for keeping income steady. I’ve done this many years, and around here everybody does it this way. Wheat gives me one harvest in June, then I turn right around and plant maize. The gap is short, so I can’t make things too complicated. I have well water, so if the rain is short I can still protect the crop, but pumping costs money, so I won’t water more than needed.

For wheat, I’ll still use an improved local variety like the ones people around here buy from the dealer. I usually sow in early October. Last year the wheat did better when I didn’t cut fertilizer too much, so this year I’ll stay around my usual rate, maybe a bit on the safe side because yellow wheat at jointing really hurts yield. I’ll put most fertilizer down before sowing, then topdress once around jointing. Wheat needs the water more, so I’ll probably irrigate about three times if rainfall is normal: one after sowing if the soil is dry, one at jointing, and one around grain filling if needed. For maize after wheat harvest, I won’t waste time with heavy tillage because the planting window is too tight. I’ll use a summer maize hybrid seed and plant right after wheat comes off in mid-June. Maize doesn’t always need as much irrigation if summer rain comes on time, so I’ll probably water once or twice depending on rain. I’ll spend the money mainly on seed, fertilizer, and herbicide first, because if weeds take over or fertilizer is too short, yield drops fast. I’m not trying anything fancy this year, just doing what has worked on my fields.
